issues.subject: Shipwright: the roadmap is not a promise
issues.text:
SHIPWRIGHT
by Nadia Kerr. Sunday {date}

View in your browser: https://shipwrightweekly.example/p/shipwright-the-roadmap-is-not-a-promise

Hello from a rainy Hebden Bridge. I'm writing this on Sunday 18 October after a week of planning sessions with two clients, both of whom had the same argument about their roadmaps. So that's the essay.

THIS WEEK'S ESSAY

The roadmap is not a promise
Both teams had shared a roadmap with customers in the spring. Both had since learned things that made half of it wrong. And both were about to ship the wrong half anyway, because the roadmap had turned into a promise somewhere along the way.

A roadmap is a statement of what you believe today about what matters next. It should get less certain the further out it looks, and it should say so. The fix I suggested to both teams was boring: three columns (now, next, later), no dates past the current quarter, and a line at the top saying when it was last changed and why.

One team took it. The other is going to print the old one on a poster for their customer day on 29 October. I'll let you know how that goes.

DECISION OF THE WEEK

Cut the export feature, keep the API
A reader's team had two weeks left and two features half done: a CSV export customers had asked for, and a public API that three partners needed. They shipped the API and told customers that export would come through it. Most of the customers who asked for export were really asking to get their data into a spreadsheet, and a partner built that in a week.

THREE THINGS I READ

How a bus company decides which routes to cut
Not about software at all, and the clearest piece on trade-offs I've read this year.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/how-a-bus-company-decides-which-routes-to-cut

The quiet cost of 'quick wins'
Twelve small features, each cheap, together doubling the support load.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/the-quiet-cost-of-quick-wins

Writing a one-page product brief
A template I've since stolen for two clients.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/writing-a-one-page-product-brief

Have a good week,
Nadia

issues.subject: Shipwright: say no in writing
issues.text:
SHIPWRIGHT
by Nadia Kerr. Sunday {date}

View in your browser: https://shipwrightweekly.example/p/shipwright-say-no-in-writing

Hello. Short essay this week, longer decision. I've been thinking about how teams turn down requests, and how often 'not now' quietly becomes 'yes, later'.

THIS WEEK'S ESSAY

Say no in writing
Most product teams say no out loud: in a meeting, in a hallway, on a call. The person who asked hears 'not right now', and a month later they ask again, because nothing was written down and nothing changed.

The teams I've seen handle this well keep a short public list of things they have decided not to do, with one line on why. It isn't a graveyard. Things come off it when the reason stops being true. But it means that the second time someone asks, the answer is a link, and the conversation starts from the reason instead of from scratch.

DECISION OF THE WEEK

Raise the price for new customers only
A small scheduling company needed more revenue and had 900 customers on a price set four years ago. Instead of a price rise for everyone, they raised it for new sign-ups and gave existing customers a year's notice. Churn was flat. Two long-time customers wrote in to say they'd been expecting it for ages.

THREE THINGS I READ

The meeting that should have been a document
With an actual template for the document.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/the-meeting-that-should-have-been-a-document

What support tickets tell you that analytics can't
A support lead on reading tickets as a product signal.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/what-support-tickets-tell-you-that-analytics-can-t

On naming features
Why the internal name always leaks, and how to pick one that can.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/on-naming-features

Until next Sunday,
Nadia

issues.subject: Shipwright: the second customer
issues.text:
SHIPWRIGHT
by Nadia Kerr. Sunday {date}

View in your browser: https://shipwrightweekly.example/p/shipwright-the-second-customer

Hello. This week I've been helping a founder decide whether to build something their biggest customer wants. The essay is what I told them.

THIS WEEK'S ESSAY

The second customer
When your largest customer asks for a feature, the question isn't whether they'll pay for it. They probably will. The question is whether a second customer will ever want it.

I ask founders to name the second customer. Not a segment, a company. If they can, build it, and talk to that second company while you do. If they can't, you're about to become that customer's agency, and every feature after this one will be easier to justify and harder to maintain.

The founder I spoke to this week named two. They're building it.

DECISION OF THE WEEK

Turn off the free plan for teams
A note-taking tool found that teams on its free plan generated a third of support tickets and almost no upgrades. They kept free for individuals and gave teams a 30-day trial instead. Sign-ups fell, revenue rose, and support response times halved within a month.

THREE THINGS I READ

Why onboarding checklists work (when they do)
Short, with data from four products.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/why-onboarding-checklists-work-when-they-do

A product manager's first 90 days, revisited
An honest follow-up to a famous plan, with what didn't work.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/a-product-manager-s-first-90-days-revisited

Pricing pages that answer the question
Twelve examples, mostly good.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/pricing-pages-that-answer-the-question

Have a good week,
Nadia

issues.subject: Shipwright: metrics that argue with each other
issues.text:
SHIPWRIGHT
by Nadia Kerr. Sunday {date}

View in your browser: https://shipwrightweekly.example/p/shipwright-metrics-that-argue-with-each-other

Hello. A reader asked me last month why their dashboard had eleven 'north star' metrics. This is a longer answer than they wanted.

THIS WEEK'S ESSAY

Metrics that argue with each other
One metric can be gamed. Two metrics that pull in opposite directions are much harder to fool. Speed and accuracy. Sign-ups and thirty-day retention. Tickets closed and tickets reopened.

I'd rather a team watch three pairs than eleven single numbers. A pair tells you what you traded away to get the improvement, which is the question every review should ask and almost none do. And it's easier to remember six numbers when they come in pairs.

DECISION OF THE WEEK

Ship the redesign to 5% for a month
A travel booking team had a finished redesign and a launch date. Their head of product made them ship it to 5% of users for a month first. Conversion was the same, but cancellations rose by a fifth: the new layout hid the refund terms. They fixed it before the full launch.

THREE THINGS I READ

Counting what doesn't happen
On measuring problems you prevented.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/counting-what-doesn-t-happen

A field guide to vanity metrics
Funny and a bit painful.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/a-field-guide-to-vanity-metrics

How a hospital chooses which software to replace
Procurement as product management.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/how-a-hospital-chooses-which-software-to-replace

Until next Sunday,
Nadia

issues.subject: Shipwright: the team that shipped every Friday
issues.text:
SHIPWRIGHT
by Nadia Kerr. Sunday {date}

View in your browser: https://shipwrightweekly.example/p/shipwright-the-team-that-shipped-every-friday

Hello. I spent a day this week with a team that releases every Friday afternoon, which goes against everything I was taught. Here's why it works for them.

THIS WEEK'S ESSAY

The team that shipped every Friday
Their reasoning is simple. Fridays are quiet for their customers, who are accountants, and the team is all in the office. If something breaks, everyone who can fix it is in the room, and nobody's weekend is ruined because the release is small.

The lesson isn't 'ship on Fridays'. It's that the right release day depends on your customers' week, not on a rule you read somewhere. Ask when your users are least busy and when your team is most present, and see where those overlap.

DECISION OF THE WEEK

Freeze features for six weeks
A payments startup had 140 open bugs and a support queue a week deep. They stopped feature work for six weeks and told their sales team why. Bug count fell to 30, and the quarter's renewals came in higher than any before.

THREE THINGS I READ

Release notes people actually read
Short, specific, with one screenshot.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/release-notes-people-actually-read

On-call for product managers
A team that puts its PMs on the rota, and what changed.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/on-call-for-product-managers

The planning fallacy, with examples
Mostly from house renovations, which felt personal.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/the-planning-fallacy-with-examples

Have a good week,
Nadia

issues.subject: Shipwright: write the announcement first
issues.text:
SHIPWRIGHT
by Nadia Kerr. Sunday {date}

View in your browser: https://shipwrightweekly.example/p/shipwright-write-the-announcement-first

Hello. An old trick this week, but I keep meeting teams who've never tried it.

THIS WEEK'S ESSAY

Write the announcement first
Before you build a feature, write the email you'll send when it ships. Two paragraphs. Who it's for, what they can now do, and why they'd care.

If you can't write it, you don't know what you're building yet. If you can write it but it sounds dull, the feature might be dull. And if two people on the team write different announcements for the same feature, you've found the disagreement before it cost you a quarter.

The best teams I know keep the draft in the project's brief and update it as they learn. On launch day, it's ready.

DECISION OF THE WEEK

Remove the setting nobody understood
A messaging app had a notification setting with four options that even the team couldn't explain. They looked at usage: 96% had never touched it. They removed it, picked the sensible default, and got three support emails about it in a month.

THREE THINGS I READ

Saying sorry in a status page
Good and bad apologies from outages this year.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/saying-sorry-in-a-status-page

The two-page strategy
A strategy document short enough to be read.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/the-two-page-strategy

Interviewing customers who left
Practical questions to ask, and ones to avoid.

Read: https://shipwrightweekly.example/r/interviewing-customers-who-left

Until next Sunday,
Nadia
